extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and practitioners authorized to practice before the USPTO (respondents in disciplinary/reciprocal-discipline proceedings); Office of Enrollment and Discipline staff
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules the USPTO Director applies when deciding whether to impose reciprocal discipline based on a state's disciplinary adjudication (37 C.F.R. § 11.24), including defenses to reciprocal discipline, nunc pro tunc requests, duties during suspension, and reinstatement rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selling standard (grounds to avoid reciprocal discipline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Selling v. Radford and 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1), reciprocal discipline is presumed proper unless the respondent clearly and convincingly demonstrates a genuine issue of material fact that: (i) the procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process; (ii) there was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject; or (iii) the imposition of the same sanction by the Office would result in a grave injustice; (iv) any argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid imposition of identical discipline, the practitioner must create a genuine issue of material fact as to one of these elements and prove it by clear and convincing evidence. The USPTO Director applies Selling and mirrors § 11.24(d)(1). Federal case law treats this as a narrow standard limiting review of state proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof: clear and convincing evidence by respondent
rubrics_metrics.description: In reciprocal-discipline cases, it is the respondent attorney's burden to demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, that one of the Selling elements precludes reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities (In re Kramer, In re Friedman, In re Zdravkovich) establish that the standard is narrow; the Director is not sitting as a court of review to relitigate state findings. The respondent must meet this heightened evidentiary standard to prevail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director shall impose identical discipline absent successful rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director shall impose the identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification unless the practitioner clearly and convincingly demonstrates a genuine issue of material fact under § 11.24(d)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The listed categories of discipline (public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, disciplinary disqualification) are to be applied identically to the state-imposed sanction unless successfully rebutted as described above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave injustice analysis: proportionality/fitting of sanction
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim of 'grave injustice' focuses on whether the severity of the state-ordered punishment 'fits' the misconduct; the inquiry is whether the punishment was so ill-fitted that reciprocal discipline would be unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court decisions cited (e.g., In re Thav, In re Kramer, In re Attorney Discipline Matter) emphasize that if a state sanction is within the appropriate range for the misconduct, it is not a grave injustice to impose it reciprocally. The USPTO looks to the state record and accepted standards (e.g., ABA Standards) to assess proportionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions provide a means for determining an appropriate disciplinary sanction and ensuring consistency across similar misconduct and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Stipulation and California order applied the ABA Standards, giving them 'great weight' and using aggravating and mitigating factors; when multiple acts specify different sanctions, the most severe sanction is applied. USPTO has referenced ABA Standards in prior disciplinary decisions when determining sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and mitigating factors in sanctioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating and mitigating factors must be considered in selecting an appropriate sanction; serious aggravating factors support harsher punishment while mitigating factors can reduce sanction severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from the record: aggravating factors included multiple statutory violations and causing significant economic loss to a bankruptcy estate; mitigating factors included years of discipline-free practice, good character, pro bono work, and the respondent's stipulation that the misconduct was aberrational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nunc pro tunc (nune pro tune) reciprocal discipline criteria (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal discipline may be imposed nunc pro tunc only if the practitioner promptly notified the OED Director of the suspension in another jurisdiction, and establishes by clear and convincing evidence that the practitioner voluntarily ceased all activities related to practice before the Office and complied with all provisions of § 11.58.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary cessation of practice alone is insufficient. The practitioner must prove prompt notice to OED and full compliance with § 11.58 (duties of disciplined practitioners) by clear and convincing evidence. Prior USPTO decisions have refused nunc pro tunc discipline where these requirements were not met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties under 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 during suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplined practitioners must comply with duties enumerated in § 11.58, which include, among other things, filing notices of withdrawal in each patent and trademark application pending before the USPTO and providing notices of the discipline to all State and Federal jurisdictions and to all clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain nunc pro tunc recognition for time served, a respondent must show compliance with § 11.58. Failure to file withdrawals or to notify jurisdictions/clients is fatal to a nunc pro tunc claim. The USPTO enforces the express terms of § 11.24(f) in evaluating such claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural response timeline to Notice and Order
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner notified under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24 is provided an opportunity to file, within forty (40) days, a response opposing imposition of reciprocal discipline based on the reasons provided in § 11.24(d)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely filing of a response is required to raise defenses under § 11.24(d)(1). Extensions may be granted, but procedures and deadlines govern the respondent's opportunity to contest reciprocal discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrelevance of ignorance of law and economic hardship as defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of ignorance of the law and claims of economic hardship are legally irrelevant defenses in reciprocal-discipline proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ignorance of the law is inconsistent with the right to advise others of the law and does not excuse failure to satisfy reporting/disciplinary requirements; economic hardship likewise is not a proper defense to disciplinary matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-discipline procedural and administrative requirements (publication, notification, dissociation, restrictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the USPTO imposes discipline, the OED Director shall publish notice in the Official Gazette, give notice pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.59 to disciplinary enforcement agencies and courts where the respondent is admitted, and ensure the respondent complies with § 11.58; the USPTO may dissociate the respondent's name from Customer Numbers/Electronic System accounts and bar obtaining or being added to a Customer Number until reinstatement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order enumerates concrete administrative steps the Office will take: publish a notice materially consistent with the provided text, give 11.59 notices to state/federal jurisdictions, dissociate names from accounts, and bar Customer Number application/use until reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement procedure and probation (37 C.F.R. § 11.60)
rubrics_metrics.description: A respondent may file a petition for reinstatement under 37 C.F.R. § 11.60 after completing the required portion of suspension (here, after completing ninety (90) days of the one-year suspension); if reinstated, a probationary period (two years in this case) commences on the date the petition is granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order specifies the timing for filing for reinstatement and the conditions of probation upon reinstatement. The petitioner must follow § 11.60 procedures for reinstatement.
